title: RTX 4090 inference latency fluctuates and can be slower than GTX 1080
body: I implemented instance segmentation with a SOLOv2 model. On my GTX 1080 with TensorRT 7.2.3.4, driver 496.49 and CUDA 11.1, processing an 832×256 image took 25–35 ms. After moving to an RTX 4090, driver 531.61 and TensorRT 8.6.0.12 while keeping CUDA 11.1, I updated deprecated interfaces and got the program running, but processing now takes 25–55 ms. The timing includes preprocessing, inference and post-processing, and the additional variation appears to come from inference. How can I make the 4090 consistently faster?

symptoms_visible: My SOLOv2 program processes an 832×256 image in 25–35 ms on the GTX 1080, but takes 25–55 ms on the RTX 4090.
The timing includes preprocessing, inference and post-processing, and the additional variation appears during inference.
N0.label: N0 fluctuating 4090 latency reported

symptoms_visible: After upgrading to CUDA 12.1, the RTX 4090 timing still fluctuates.
The same TensorRT 8 code takes about 25 ms without fluctuations on another GTX 1080, while the GPU timing shown by Nsight Systems fluctuates on the RTX 4090.
N1_x.label: N1_x CUDA upgrade aftermath

symptoms_visible: My application still fluctuates, while the trtexec output reports a median single-inference latency of 3.48633 ms.
N2.label: N2 isolated trtexec benchmark collected

symptoms_visible: When I repeatedly call executeV2 on one image, the printed time starts around 2.9 ms and later rises to about 10 ms.
The measured copyOutputToHost time also increases.
When I remove OpenCV minAreaRect and replace matrix multiplication with a loop, copyOutputToHost no longer becomes slower.
N3.label: N3 application latency growth localized

symptoms_visible: After changing the inference call to enqueueV3, TensorRT timing still varies when the post-processing code runs.
N4_x.label: N4_x enqueueV3 aftermath

symptoms_visible: With the RTX 4090 clock locked to 3120 MHz, the timing fluctuation disappears and processing one image takes about 20 ms, faster than on the GTX 1080.
N_terminal.label: N_terminal stable latency with fixed GPU clock

symptoms_visible: With the RTX 4090 clock locked to 3120 MHz, the timing fluctuation disappears and processing one image takes about 20 ms, faster than on the GTX 1080.
N_terminal_shortcut.label: N_terminal_shortcut direct clock-fix resolution

solution.intent: Upgrade the RTX 4090 environment to CUDA 12 while retaining TensorRT 8.6, then profile the workload with Nsight Systems.
solution.concrete_example: Install CUDA 12 for the RTX 4090 and TensorRT 8.6 environment, then inspect the workload in Nsight Systems to see where GPU time is being spent.

edges.comment: Issue c1-c3, reporter's RTX 4090 system: the reporter upgraded to CUDA 12.1 and captured an Nsight Systems trace, but the timing continued to fluctuate. The same TensorRT 8 code was stable on another GTX 1080, so the CUDA upgrade was not the resolution.

question_patterns: Could you run the ONNX model with trtexec and share the complete performance output?
Please benchmark the model with trtexec so we can compare isolated TensorRT latency with your application.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I ran my model with trtexec and attached the complete output. It reports a median latency of 3.48633 ms for a single inference.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The trtexec latency itself repeatedly rises from about 3 ms to more than 10 ms during the isolated benchmark.
The median is about 3.6 ms instead of 3.48633 ms, with otherwise similar output.

edges.comment: Issue c4-c7, reporter's RTX 4090 system: the maintainer requested a trtexec benchmark and the reporter supplied six screenshots of raw output. The 3.48633 ms median is read directly from that output; judging the isolated benchmark as stable is engineer-side inference.

question_patterns: Can you compare the isolated latency with repeated inference inside your application and share the timings?
What happens to the inference-call latency as the application loop continues?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I looped one image through executeV2 and printed the time. It starts at about 2.9 ms, close to the trtexec result, but later increases significantly to about 10 ms. I attached the timing output.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The executeV2 loop remains near 3 ms throughout; only CPU preprocessing time increases.
The loop begins near 3.1 ms and occasionally reaches 9 ms rather than 10 ms.

edges.comment: Issue c7-c11, reporter's RTX 4090 application: in response to the latency comparison request, the reporter measured repeated executeV2 calls. The reporter then volunteered that TensorRT 7 used execute, TensorRT 8 used executeV2, copyOutputToHost also grew, and OpenCV post-processing operations changed the observed timing.

solution.intent: Replace executeV2 with enqueueV3 and use explicit stream synchronization to avoid interactions caused by the default CUDA stream.
solution.concrete_example: Submit inference with enqueueV3 on an explicit CUDA stream and synchronize that stream at the point where the output is required instead of relying on executeV2's default-stream behavior.

edges.comment: Issue c12-c15, reporter's RTX 4090 application: the maintainer suspected default-stream interaction and recommended enqueueV3 with explicit synchronization. The reporter changed to enqueueV3 but still observed post-processing-associated TensorRT timing variation, so this API change was not the complete resolution.

solution.intent: Stabilize the RTX 4090's GPU clock instead of attributing the application-only latency growth to TensorRT inference, then rerun the complete pipeline to verify stable latency.
solution.concrete_example: Lock the RTX 4090 GPU clock at the tested 3120 MHz setting, rerun the same image loop and complete preprocessing/inference/post-processing pipeline, and confirm that latency no longer drifts before declaring the issue resolved.
solution.inference_hint: The reporter supplied the raw trtexec result, loop timings and the successful 3120 MHz clock-lock test. Interpreting the stable isolated TensorRT benchmark plus application-only drift as dynamic GPU clock behavior is the diagnostic inference accepted by the maintainer in c16.

edges.comment: Issue c15-c17, original reporter's RTX 4090 problem: the reporter locked the GPU clock to 3120 MHz, after which fluctuations disappeared and total processing fell to 20 ms. The maintainer endorsed fixing the GPU clocks and the reporter agreed to close. Comments c18-c22 concern a later multi-GPU clock-management problem and are deliberately not spliced into this opening RTX 4090 chain.

solution.intent: Stabilize the RTX 4090's GPU clock and verify the complete pipeline directly, without first treating the CUDA version or TensorRT execution API as the resolution.
solution.concrete_example: Lock the RTX 4090 GPU clock at the tested 3120 MHz setting and rerun the full image-processing loop; confirm that the 25–55 ms variation disappears and that total latency is consistently below the GTX 1080 result.

edges.comment: Shortcut required because the thread's first proposed environment upgrade was falsified. This edge lets an agent propose the ultimately verified GPU-clock stabilization immediately, while requiring a full-pipeline retest before resolution.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify dynamic RTX 4090 GPU clock behavior as the accepted cause of the latency fluctuation and recommend fixing or locking the GPU clock.

The diagnosis must be grounded in the collected contrast: isolated trtexec latency is near 3.49 ms, while repeated application execution grows from about 2.9 ms to about 10 ms and is affected by surrounding post-processing workload.
Must not present upgrading to CUDA 12.1 as the fix; the fluctuation continued after that upgrade.
Must not present switching from executeV2 to enqueueV3 as the complete fix; the reporter still observed the variation after making that change.
Must ask the reporter to verify the complete pipeline after stabilizing the clock and treat the original issue as resolved only after the reported fluctuation disappears and total latency improves.

persona_hint.experience_level: Intermediate C++/CUDA and TensorRT user who can migrate deprecated APIs, run trtexec and Nsight Systems, edit inference and post-processing code, and adjust GPU clocks, but needs help interpreting cross-component timing behavior.
persona_hint.communication_style: Cooperative and experiment-driven; shares screenshots and exact timings, tests suggestions promptly, proposes hypotheses, and reports unexpected interactions in detail.
